query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms several primary non-eutectic phases during solidification and exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence. Under rapid cooling, slower cooling, and subsequent reheating assessed by thermal analysis, what single intervention could increase amorphous retention and thermal stability while overcoming extensive primary crystallization? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the alloy’s reported glass formation and crystallization behavior, the relevant cooling-rate and reheating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled subcritical thermal pulse applied immediately after ultra-rapid melt spinning induces a glass-to-glass transition in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, leading to enhanced amorphous retention and increased thermal stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 sample produced via melt-spinning at cooling rates of approximately 10⁵–10⁶ K/s.
generation.intervention: Expose the as-quenched sample to a short-duration (30–60 seconds) thermal pulse at a temperature just below the crystallization onset (around Tg + 10 K, e.g., 750–800 K) in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The thermal pulse is applied immediately after melt-spinning using a controlled furnace or alternative heating device; the sample is maintained in an inert gas environment to prevent oxidation, and subsequent reheating during testing is limited to below ~960 K.
generation.structural_mediator: A glass-to-glass transition mediated by controlled atomic rearrangement and enhanced short-/medium-range ordering, leading to a lower-energy amorphous state.
generation.mechanism: The subcritical thermal pulse provides sufficient energy for atomic mobility to relax internal stresses and eliminate nascent nucleation sites without crossing the crystallization threshold, thus kinetically stabilizing the amorphous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to as-melt-spun samples, the thermally pulsed samples will exhibit an increased onset temperature for crystallization (by roughly 50 K) and greater resistance to primary crystallization during subsequent thermal cycling.
generation.baseline: Melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 samples processed without any post-quench thermal intervention, which tend to show primary crystallization upon slower reheating.
generation.boundary: Cooling rate: ≥10⁵ K/s; Thermal pulse temperature: approximately 750–800 K; Reheating during testing must remain below about 960 K to avoid triggering crystallization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal pulse temperature and duration may vary; if the pulse exceeds the safe temperature range or is too long, unintended crystallization may occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 samples. Apply the subcritical thermal pulse to one group while leaving the other as a control. Conduct DSC analysis and repeat controlled reheating cycles, complemented by XRD and TEM characterization.
measurements: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to determine onset crystallization temperatures
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally pulsed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature or if they develop similar levels of crystalline phases as the control samples upon reheating, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. AbstractGlass-to-glass transitions are useful for us to understand the glass nature, but it remains difficult to tune the metallic glass into significantly different glass states. Here, we have demonstrated that the high-entropy can enhance the degree of disorder in an equiatomic high-entropy metallic glass NbNiZrTiCo and elevate it to a high-energy glass state. An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures. Dramatic atomic rearrangement with a short- and medium-range ordering is revealed by in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction analyses. This glass-to-glass transition leads to a significant improvement in the modulus, hardness, and thermal stability, all of which could promote their applications. Based on the proposed high-entropy effect, two high-entropy metallic glasses are developed and they show similar glass-to-glass transitions. Three exothermic peaks are observed at 781, 911, and 1016 K in the DSC curve with released heats of 1.65, 1.27, and 1.59 kJ mol−1, respectively. No obvious glass transition temperature (Tg) is observed in the conventional DSC curve of the as-prepared sample. The Tg of the as-prepared sample can be observed before the first exothermic peak with heating rates higher than 1000 K s−1 by Flash DSC (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 7). papers.approach: Systematic variation of cooling conditions – slow cooling (~52 K/s on copper plate), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (~3018 K/s), and ultra‐rapid quenching via melt-spinning (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) – with subsequent thermal analysis including DSC and thermography.
papers.findings: Slow cooling yields a complex, multi‐phase crystalline microstructure comprising several primary non‐eutectic phases; accelerated cooling reduces the number of phases; ultra‐rapid cooling produces an amorphous structure. Phosphorus addition is shown to broaden the solidification range, reduce transformation temperatures, and enhance glass‐forming ability.
papers.mechanism: High cooling rates suppress nucleation and growth of crystalline phases by increasing undercooling, while phosphorus modifies the solidification pathway by lowering transformation temperatures and promoting amorphization via kinetic stabilization.

papers.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.
papers.system: NbNiZrTiCo metallic glass (as a high-entropy metallic glass exemplar)
papers.approach: Isothermal annealing experiments and Flash DSC analysis on the as-prepared amorphous state to induce a glass-to-glass transition while monitoring heat release and structural changes via synchrotron XRD.
papers.findings: A significant glass-to-glass transformation is observed upon reheating the alloy just above the glass transition (but below crystallization), with an enormous exothermic event that leads to a lower-energy, thermally stabilized amorphous state. The low-energy state shows improved mechanical properties and enhanced thermal stability against crystallization.
papers.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in the alloy helps to trap a high-energy glass state during quenching; strategic subcritical reheating permits atomic rearrangement into a more stable amorphous configuration without triggering full crystallization.

papers.title: Exploring the Phase Space of Multi-Principal-Element Alloys and Predicting the Formation of Bulk Metallic Glasses.
papers.system: Various multi-principal-element alloys (with focus on predicting glass-forming compositions)
papers.approach: Computational and experimental evaluation of bulk metallic glass formation, including empirical estimation of critical cooling rates, exploration via random algorithms, and analysis of compositional effects (including the presence of deep eutectics) on glass formation.
papers.findings: Critical cooling rates vary widely among systems; in phosphorus-containing HEAs, lower critical cooling rates (achievable by melt-spinning or similar methods) are correlated with successful amorphization. The predictions align well with experimental observations in systems like Cu-Zr-Ti and Pd-Ni-P.
papers.mechanism: An increase in configurational entropy reduces Gibbs free energy of the amorphous phase; controlling cooling kinetics (by targeting specific cooling rate windows) can kinetically suppress crystallization while promoting glass retention.

mechanisms: Kinetic suppression: High cooling rates reduce the time available for nucleation and growth of crystalline phases, favoring amorphous retention.
Phosphorus effect: Phosphorus addition decreases the effective solidification temperature range and promotes undercooling, thereby aiding in the formation of amorphous structures.
Entropy stabilization: High configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the amorphous state and destabilizes potential crystalline ordering.

Reheating-induced relaxation: Carefully controlled subcritical reheating can trigger atomic rearrangement into a lower-energy, thermodynamically more stabilized amorphous state without crossing the crystallization threshold.
disagreements: The relative importance of kinetic versus thermodynamic control in stabilizing the amorphous phase is debated, with some works emphasizing the necessity of ultra-rapid cooling while others point to the benefits of post-quench thermal processing.

There is variation in the reported transformation temperatures and undercooling extents across different cooling methods, suggesting that the interplay between cooling rate, alloy composition, and reheating protocol is not yet fully resolved.

candidates.changes: Highlighted the need for precise control of temperature and duration in the subcritical thermal pulse to prevent unintended crystallization. Reiterated the applicability of the glass-to-glass transition mechanism to the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 system.
